title_eng: Machine learning-based sample misidentification error detection in clinical laboratory tests: A retrospective multicenter study
abstract:
Machine Learning-Based Sample Misidentification Error 
Detection in Clinical Laboratory Tests: A Retrospective 
Multicenter Study
Hyeon Seok Seok 
 ,a,b Shinae Yu 
 ,c Kyung-Hwa Shin 
 ,d Woochang Lee 
 ,e Sail Chun 
 ,e
Sollip Kim 
 ,e,*,† and Hangsik Shin 
 b,*,†
BACKGROUND: In clinical laboratories, the precision 
and sensitivity of autoverification technologies are cru -
cial for ensuring reliable diagnostics. Conventional 
methods have limited sensitivity and applicability, mak-
ing error detection challenging and reducing laboratory 
efficiency. This study introduces a machine learning 
(ML)-based autoverification technology to enhance tu -
mor marker test error detection.
METHODS: The effectiveness of various ML models was 
evaluated by analyzing a large data set of 397 751 for 
model training and internal validation and 215 339 for 
external validation. Sample misidentification was simu -
lated by random shuffling error-free test results with a 
1% error rate to achieve a real-world approximation. 
The ML models were developed with Bayesian opti -
mization for tuning. Model validation was performed 
internally at the primary institution and externally at 
other institutions, comparing the ML models’ perform-
ance with conventional delta check methods.
RESULTS: Deep neural networks and extreme gradient 
boosting achieved an area under the receiver operating 
characteristic curve of 0.834 to 0.903, outperforming 
that of conventional methods (0.705 to 0.816). 
External validation by 3 independent laboratories 
showed that the balanced accuracy of the ML model ran-
ged from 0.760 to 0.836, outperforming the balanced 
accuracy of 0.670 to 0.773 of the conventional models.
CONCLUSIONS: This study addresses limitations regard-
ing the sensitivity of current delta check methods for de-
tection of sample misidentification errors and provides 
versatile models that mitigate the operational challenges 
faced by smaller laboratories. Our findings offer a path-
way toward more efficient and reliable clinical laboratory 
testing.

Introduction
During clinical laboratory testing, errors can occur in every 
process. These errors are mostly detected during the test-
ing process and appropriately addressed in the clinical la-
boratory. For example, laboratories can reject the sample 
and/or proceed with the test while including a note regard-
ing the sample issue in the report ( 1). However, despite 
being rare (accounting for 0.3% of preanalytical errors), 
misidentification errors are difficult to detect and can 
lead to serious diagnostic and therapeutic mistakes (2).
To detect errors, clinical laboratories employ a mul-
tistep strategy to verify results before reporting. The 
most commonly used method is a delta check, which 
warns laboratory personnel of potential errors when 
the difference between the last and current test results 
exceeds a certain threshold. However, the sensitivity of 
the conventional delta check method remains relatively 
low (approximately 20% to 50%) ( 3, 4). The main 
reason for this low sensitivity is the fact that current 
methods rely on outlier processing, which removes the 
extremes of the delta distribution. However, relying on 
outlier processing is unlikely to reflect interindividual 
variability and may not fully reflect the different envir -
onments of laboratories; thus, high accuracy cannot be 
expected. To overcome this limitation, we previously 
evaluated a machine learning (ML)-based delta check 
method and observed that ML-based delta check models 
for several tumor markers outperformed conventional

methods (5). Although this study took a significant step 
in confirming the feasibility of ML in detecting tumor 
marker misidentification errors, the focus was on intern-
al validation, and an assessment of generalizability was 
lacking. Thus, to determine whether this approach can 
be universally used in real-world clinical settings, exter-
nal validation is required to ensure reliable results (6).
This study aimed to develop ML-based delta check 
models and verify their utility and generalizability in a 
multicenter comparative study. To this end, we con-
structed data sets of tumor markers from the clinical la-
boratories of multiple general hospitals, compared the 
results of conventional delta check methods with those 
of ML-based delta check models, and examined the in-
ternal and external validation results for each laboratory 
to robustly evaluate the usefulness and generalizability of 
ML models in the clinical autoverification process. A 
schematic representation of the methodology applied 
in this study is provided in Fig. 1.
Methods
DATA SET
The laboratory test results were collected retrospectively 
from Asan Medical Center (AMC, Seoul, Republic of 
Korea) for model training and internal validation, and 
from Haeundae Paik Hospital (HPH, Busan, Republic 
of Korea), Pusan National University Hospital (PNU, 
Busan, Republic of Korea), and Ilsan Paik Hospital 
(IPH, Goyang, Republic of Korea) for external valid-
ation. The study protocols were approved by the ethics 
review boards of each institution, and consent from hu-
man participants was waived due to the nature of the 
retrospective study (AMC 2022-1699, HPH 2022- 
09-017, PNU 2210-023-120, and IPH 2022-09-031). 
The data collected represented the current and previous 
test results for the tumor markers alpha-fetoprotein 
(AFP), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA19-9), carcinoembryo-
nic antigen (CEA), and prostate-specific antigen 
(PSA), sex, and age, where the previous test result was 
only collected if it was measured within 2 years of the 
current test result. An Alinity-I (Abbott Laboratories) 
for AMC and a Roche Cobas C-8000 (Roche 
Diagnostics GmbH) for HPH, PNU, and IPH were 
used for tumor marker testing. The initially collected 
data were manually reviewed to exclude missing test re-
sults, study participants under 20 years of age, and test 
results reported in different ways in different laboratories 
(e.g., test result values exceeding the analytical measure-
ment intervals of the instrument) before analysis. The 
total numbers of samples consisting of previous–current 
paired test results were 397 751, 108 088, 89 902, and 
17 349 for AMC, HPH, PNU, and IPH, respectively, 
and different numbers of samples were obtained for 
each tumor marker. Details of the number of samples 
obtained for each tumor marker are provided in Table 1.
For the development and validation of the ML 
models and conventional delta check methods for sam-
ple misidentification error detection, the data set was 
partitioned as follows: 80% of the data was allocated 
to the training set, while 20% was reserved for the val-
idation data set for each tumor marker. For example, 
80% of randomly selected data from AMC’s AFP 
data set was used as the training data set to develop 
the AMC model for AFP, and the remaining 20% of 
the data was used as the validation data set for the in-
ternal validation of the AMC model for AFP; data 
sets from other laboratories (HPH, PNU, and IPH) 
were used as an external validation data set. For each 
of the other tumor markers, we developed AMC models 
in the same way. 
IN SILICO SAMPLE MISIDENTIFICATION ERROR SIMULATION
The data used in this study were retrospectively collected 
from electronic medical records, with results reported to 
clinicians after final manual verification by clinical ex-
perts. We assumed this data to be error-free because no 
abnormalities were observed during the actual clinical 
process after the results were reported. Therefore, we de-
veloped error detection ML models with artificially gener-
ated sample misidentification errors by randomly 
shuffling a part of the test results and validated the per-
formance of ML models and the delta percent check 
(DPC) and absolute DPC (absDPC) methods. The 
DPC was calculated as the ratio of the difference between 
the previous and current test results divided by the 
previous test result, and the absDPC was calculated as 
the absolute value of DPC (7). To reproduce sample mis-
identification errors, a percentage of the current test re-
sults of tumor marker test samples that consisted of 
previous–current test result pairs were randomly shuffled. 
Based on the sample misidentification error simulation, 
samples with randomly shuffled current test result values 
were labeled as misidentified (=1) samples, while samples 
without shuffling were labeled as correctly identified (=0) 
samples. Although the occurrence of misidentification er-
rors in patients’ samples can vary by laboratory size, test 
type, and patient characteristics, it is generally believed 
to be in the range of 0.1% to 5% (8–11) and has been 
reported to be approximately 1% for general laboratory 
tests (9). Therefore, considering the error rate in a typical 
clinical environment, we set the error rate to 1% in both 
the training and validation tests. However, when develop-
ing the ML models, an over-sampling technique was ap-
plied to the “misidentified class” for the effective learning 
of the ML models by balancing the number of samples 
of “correctly identified” and “misidentified” (12, 13). 
Meanwhile, for deriving delta check limits for the DPC 
and the absDPC, error simulation was not applied.
